parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -archia, from Ancient Greek ἀρχός (arkhós, “leader”).
From Latin -graphia, going back to Ancient Greek γράφειν (gráphein, “write”).
From Latin -idēs m (patronymic suffix; plural: -idae), from Ancient Greek -ίδης m (-ídēs, patronymic suffix; plural: -ίδαι (-ídai)).
From Latin -is f (genitive: -idis), from Ancient Greek -ῐς f (-ĭs) (genitive: -ῐδος (-ĭdos); plural: -ῐδες (-ĭdes)).
Learned borrowing from Latin -ismus, from Ancient Greek -ῐσμός (-ĭsmós).
Borrowed from Latin -ista, reinforced by French -iste.

parole.significato: -ite (used to form names of certain peoples, followers or descendants of a person, etc.)
parole.testo: From Latin -īta, -ītēs, from Ancient Greek -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs). Though not originally related, both ancient and modern uses of this ending often reflect the Semitic nisba suffix (whence also German -i as in Iraki, Israeli).
From Latin -o-.
Borrowed from Latin -phila, from Ancient Greek φίλος (phílos, “dear, beloved”).
Borrowed from Latin -phobus, from Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos).

parole.significato: abacus (table with balls on wires or counters in groves, for counting)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abacus, genitive and plural abacī.
From Middle High German abt, from Old High German abbat, borrowed from Late Latin abbas. Doublet of Abate.

parole.significato: The condition abulia, absence of will-power or decisiveness
parole.testo: From New Latin abūlia, from Ancient Greek ἀβουλῐ́ᾱ (aboulĭ́ā, “ill-advisedness, thoughtlessness”).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin agapē.
Derived from Latin acācia.
From Latin acephalus, from Ancient Greek ἀκέφαλος (aképhalos).

parole.significato: acolyte, altar boy (generally, an assistant who performs liturgical duties such as carrying the wine, water and lights…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin acolythus, from Ancient Greek ἀκόλουθος (akólouthos, “follower, helper”).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin acribia (18th c.), from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓κρῑ́βειᾰ (ăkrī́beiă), from ἀκριβής (akribḗs, “accurate, precise”). Compare Italian acribia.

From Middle High German alabaster, derived from Latin alabastrum, from Ancient Greek ἀλάβαστρος (alábastros), from earlier ἀλάβαστος (alábastos, “alabaster vase”). Cognate with Gothic 𐌰𐌻𐌰𐌱𐌰𐌻𐍃𐍄𐍂𐌰𐌿𐌽 (alabalstraun).

parole.significato: Alan (a member of the Iranian nomadic people of the Alans)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Alānī, from Ancient Greek Ἀλανοί (Alanoí).
Borrowed from Latin amarantus, from Ancient Greek ἀμάραντος (amárantos, “unfading”). The spelling Amaranth (as in English) is due to the influence of ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”).
From Latin Amaryllis (“a country girl in Virgil's Eclogues”), from Ancient Greek Ἀμαρυλλίς (Amarullís, from ἀμαρύσσω (amarússō, “to shine”)).
Borrowed from New Latin amblyōpia, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓μβλῠωπῐ́ᾱ (ămblŭōpĭ́ā).
Borrowed from Latin amnēstia, from Ancient Greek ἀμνηστία (amnēstía).
Latin amnestia < Ancient Greek ἀμνηστία (amnēstía, “forgetfulness, pardon”)
Borrowed from Latin amnion, from Ancient Greek ἀμνίον (amníon).

parole.significato: amphora (a two handled jar with a narrow neck)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin amphora, from Ancient Greek ἀμφορεύς (amphoreús).
From Latin anadiplōsis, from Ancient Greek ἀναδίπλωσις (anadíplōsis).
Borrowed from Latin analogia, from Ancient Greek ἀναλογία (analogía).
Borrowed from Latin analysis.
From Late Latin anamnēsis, from Ancient Greek ἀνάμνησις (anámnēsis, “calling to mind, reminiscence”), from ἀνα- (ana-) + μιμνήσκω (mimnḗskō, “to remind, remember”).
Borrowed from Latin anapaestus, from Ancient Greek ἀνάπαιστος (anápaistos).

parole.significato: Anatomy, study of the structure of living beings.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin anatomia, from Ancient Greek ἀνατομία (anatomía), from ἀνατομή (anatomḗ, “dissection”), from ἀνά (aná, “up”) + τέμνω (témnō, “to cut, incise”).
From Middle High German anīs (“anise”), from Latin anīsum.
From Latin anthracītis, from Ancient Greek ἀνθρακῖτις (anthrakîtis).
From Latin antidotum, from Ancient Greek ἀντίδοτος (antídotos, “antidote, remedy”), from ἀντιδίδωμι (antidídōmi, “I give in return, repay”).
From Latin antinomia, from Ancient Greek ἀντινομία (antinomía).
From Latin antipathia, from Ancient Greek ἀντιπάθεια (antipátheia).
Late Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀντίποδες (antípodes), from ἀντί (antí, “against”) + πόδες (pódes), nominative plural of πούς (poús, “foot”).
From Late Latin antitheticus, from Ancient Greek ἀντιθετικός (antithetikós).
Borrowed from Latin aoristus, from Ancient Greek ἀόριστος (aóristos).
Learned borrowing from Latin aphaeresis, from Ancient Greek ἀφαίρεσις (aphaíresis, “a taking away”), from ἀφαιρέω (aphairéō). Doublet of Apherese
From the Latin apodīcticus (“proving clearly”, “demonstrative”), from Ancient Greek ἀποδεικτικός (apodeiktikós, “affording proof”, “demonstrative”), from ἀποδείκνυμι (apodeíknumi, “to demonstrate”).
Learned borrowing from Latin apocope, from Ancient Greek ἀποκοπή (apokopḗ).
From Latin apocryphus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόκρυφος (apókruphos).
From Late Latin apologeticum, from Ancient Greek απολογητικόν (apologētikón), from ἀπολογεῖσθαι (apologeîsthai). By surface analysis, apologetisch + -ik
From Latin apologēticus, from Ancient Greek ἀπολογητικός (apologētikós).
From Late Latin poplexia, apoplexia, from Ancient Greek ἀποπληξίᾱ (apoplēxíā), from ἀποπλήσσω (apoplḗssō, “to cripple by a stroke”); ἀπο- (apo-, “from”) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “to strike”).
From Old High German apostolo, from Latin apostolus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστολος (apóstolos).
From Late Latin archaicus, itself from Ancient Greek ἀρχαϊκός (arkhaïkós).
Borrowed from Latin archetypum, from Ancient Greek ἀρχέτυπον (arkhétupon, “model, pattern”).
Borrowed from Latin architectus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn).
From Late Latin archīvum (“public records office”).
From Latin archaeologia, from Ancient Greek ἀρχαιολογίᾱ (arkhaiologíā).

From Medieval Latin aristocratia, from Ancient Greek ἀριστοκρατίᾱ (aristokratíā, “the rule of the best“, that is, “the best-born”, “nobility”), equivalent to Ancient Greek ἄριστος (áristos, “best”) + -kratie.

From Middle High German aritmetica, borrowing from Latin arithmētica, arithmeticus, from Ancient Greek ἀριθμητική (τέχνη) (arithmētikḗ (tékhnē), “(art of) counting”), feminine of ἀριθμητικός (arithmētikós, “arithmetical”), from ἀριθμός (arithmós, “number, counting”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ri-d
Learned borrowing from Latin arcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀρκτικός (arktikós).
From Latin arōmaticus, from Ancient Greek ἀρωματικός (arōmatikós). By surface analysis, Aroma + -isch.

parole.significato: doctor, physician (male or of unspecified gender) (without necessarily having a postgraduate degree)
parole.testo: From Middle High German arzet, arzāt, from Old High German arzāt, from Latin archīāter (“physician”), from Ancient Greek ἀρχίατρος (arkhíatros), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-) + ἰατρός (iatrós).
From Late Latin astralis, from Latin astrum (“star”) + -ālis, the first element from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron, “star”).
Borrowed from Latin astronomus, from Ancient Greek ἀστρονόμος (astronómos)
Borrowed from Latin asylum.

parole.significato: asymptote (straight line which a curve approaches arbitrarily closely)
parole.testo: From Latin asymptōta, from the feminine of Ancient Greek ἀσύμπτωτος (asúmptōtos).
From New Latin atmosphaera, from Ancient Greek ἀτμός (atmós, “steam”) + σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “sphere”).
Borrowed from Latin atomus, from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (átomos).
Derived from Latin Atticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀττῐκός (Attĭkós).
Learned borrowing from Latin aura, ultimately from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra).

parole.significato: autograph (a manuscript or document written in its author's or composer's hand)
parole.testo: From Latin autographum, from Ancient Greek αὐτόγραφος (autógraphos). By surface analysis, auto- + -graph.
From Latin axiōma, Ancient Greek ἀξίωμα (axíōma)
From New Latin azalea, from Ancient Greek ἀζαλέος (azaléos).
Borrowed from New Latin bacterium.
Borrowed from Latin barbarus.

parole.significato: base (compound that will neutralize an acid)
parole.testo: 19th c., backformation from Basen, plural of Basis, from Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis).
From Late Latin basilicum, from Ancient Greek βᾰσῐλῐκός (băsĭlĭkós).

From Middle High German basis (13th c.), from Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis). At first in various technical senses. The generalization as “foundation” likely influenced by French base, the military use probably after English base, both from the same Latin noun.
From Middle High German bërtram, bërhtram, from Old High German bërhtram, from Latin pyrethrum and influenced by the male given name, from Ancient Greek πύρεθρον (púrethron).

parole.significato: beryllium; the chemical element and alkaline earth metal with the atomic number 4
parole.testo: From New Latin bēryllium, from bēryllus, from Ancient Greek βήρυλλος (bḗrullos, “beryl”).
From Middle High German bezirc, from be- + zirc, from Latin circus, itself from Ancient Greek κίρκος (kírkos, “circle, ring”).
Learned borrowing from Latin bibliothēca, from Ancient Greek βῐβλῐοθήκη (bĭblĭothḗkē).

From Latin bīlis (“bile”) + Ancient Greek κυάνεος (kuáneos, “dark blue”) + -in. The German word was naturalized into other languages as international scientific vocabulary (e.g., bilicyanin, bilicyanine).
Borrowed from Latin blasphēmia.
Borrowed from Latin bolis.
Borrowed from Latin bronchia, from Ancient Greek βρόγχια (brónkhia).
Borrowed from Latin chamaeleōn, from Ancient Greek χᾰμαιλέων (khămailéōn).
From Latin chaos, from Ancient Greek χάος (kháos). Cognate with English chaos. Doublet of Gas.

parole.significato: character; the totality of someone's personal qualities
parole.testo: From Middle High German karacter, from Latin character, from Ancient Greek χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr, “type, nature, character”), from χαράσσω (kharássō, “to engrave”).
From Late Latin cherūb, from Ancient Greek χερούβ (kheroúb), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew כְּרוּב (kerúv).
Borrowed from Latin chīrographum.

parole.significato: surgeon (kind of doctor, male or of unspecified sex)
parole.testo: 15th century, from Latin chīrūrgus, from Ancient Greek χειρουργός (kheirourgós).
From Latin cholera (“bilious disease”), from Ancient Greek χολέρα (kholéra, “cholera”).
From Latin chrīstiānismus, from Ancient Greek χρῑστιᾱνισμός (khrīstiānismós).
From Latin chrysoberyllus, from Ancient Greek χρῡσοβήρυλλος (khrūsobḗrullos, “gold beryl”).
From Latin cȳaneus, from Ancient Greek κυάνεος (kuáneos).

From Middle High German datel, dactel, from Old High German dahtil, from Latin dactylus, from Ancient Greek δάκτυλος (dáktulos, literally “finger”), a folk-etymological alteration of a Semitic word; compare Hebrew דֶּקֶל (deqel). First attested in the 11th century CE form dahtilboum (“date tree”).

From Middle High German dūge (13th c.), from Latin duga, doga, from Ancient Greek δοχή (dokhḗ). Cognate with Dutch duig. The form with -b- appears in the 15th century. It may have been influenced by Old French dove, from the same source. However, such influence is not certain. Intervocalic -b- and -
From Latin dēmagōgia, from Ancient Greek δημαγωγίᾱ (dēmagōgíā).
From Latin diagōnālis, from Ancient Greek διαγώνιος (diagṓnios, “from angle to angle”).
From Ecclesiastical Latin diāconus, from Ancient Greek διᾱ́κονος (diā́konos).
Borrowed from Latin dialectos f, from Ancient Greek διάλεκτος f (diálektos).
From Late Latin dialogus, from Ancient Greek διάλογος (diálogos).
Borrowed from Late Latin diaphragma.
From New Latin diastole, itself based on Ancient Greek διαστολή (diastolḗ, “separation, drawing asunder”).
From Ecclesiastical Latin dicastērium, from Ancient Greek δῐκᾰστήρῐον (dĭkăstḗrĭon).

parole.significato: dilemma, predicament, quandary, conundrum, pickle, catch-22 (a situation with two (or more) alternatives to choose from…
parole.testo: From Latin dilēmma, Ancient Greek δίλημμα (dílēmma)
Borrowed from Latin distichus, from Ancient Greek δίστιχος (dístikhos).
Borrowed from Latin diaeta, from Ancient Greek δίαιτα (díaita).
From Ecclesiastical Latin dioecesis, from Ancient Greek διοίκησις (dioíkēsis).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin dosis, from Ancient Greek δόσις (dósis, “a portion prescribed”, literally “a giving”), from Proto-Hellenic *dótis, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₃tis.
From Medieval Latin doxologia, from Ancient Greek δοξολογία (doxología, “a praising”).
Borrowed from Late Latin drāma, from Ancient Greek δρᾶμα (drâma, “play, drama”, noun), from δρᾰ́ω (drắō, “do, act”, verb) + -μᾰ (-mă, nominalizing suffix). First attested in the 16th century.
Borrowed from Latin dynastēs, from Ancient Greek δυνάστης (dunástēs).
16th century, from Latin dynastīa, from Ancient Greek δυναστεία (dunasteía). Usual since the 18th century, probably reinforced by French dynastie.
Borrowed from Latin daemōn, borrowed from Ancient Greek δαίμων (daímōn).
From Latin ēchō, from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ).

parole.significato: only-begotten, sole of God the Son, denoting that he is the only and unique son of God the Father
parole.testo: ein (“one”) + geboren (“born”), a calque of Latin ūnigenitus and Ancient Greek μονογενής (monogenḗs).

parole.significato: Elysium (home of the blessed after death)
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek Ἠλῠ́σῐον (Πεδῐ́ον) (Ēlŭ́sĭon (Pedĭ́on)).
15th century, from Latin embryo, from Ancient Greek ἔμβρυον (émbruon).

parole.significato: empirical knowledge; knowledge based on testing and experience
parole.testo: From Latin empīria, from Ancient Greek ἐμπειρία (empeiría).
Borrowed from Latin empīricus, from Ancient Greek ἐμπειρικός (empeirikós).
From Latin entelechia, from Ancient Greek ἐντελέχεια (entelékheia).
Borrowed from Late Latin enthusiasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιασμός (enthousiasmós).
Borrowed from Latin epiglottis.
Since the 19th century. Compare Latin epilēpticus, Ancient Greek ἐπιληπτικός (epilēptikós).

parole.significato: epithet (word in the scientific name of a taxon following the name of the genus or species)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin epitheton, from Ancient Greek ἐπίθετον (epítheton).
Derived from Latin epitomē, derived from Ancient Greek ἐπῐτομή (epĭtomḗ).

Borrowed from Latin eremita, from Ancient Greek ἐρημίτης (erēmítēs, “person of the desert”) from ἐρημία (erēmía, “desert, solitude”), from ἔρημος (érēmos) or ἐρῆμος (erêmos, “uninhabited”) plus -ίτης (-ítēs, “one connected to, a member of”).
From Erethismus (“overexcitement, erethism”), borrowed from New Latin erethismus, from Ancient Greek ἐρεθισμός (erethismós), from ἐρεθίζειν (erethízein, “to irritate”).
Borrowed from New Latin erythēma, from Ancient Greek ἐρύθημα (erúthēma, “a redness or flush on the skin”), from ἐρυθρός (eruthrós, “red”).
From Middle High German erz-, erze-, from Old High German erzi-, from Late Latin archi-, from Ancient Greek ἀρχι- (arkhi-).

parole.significato: screed, floor made of cement or plaster (as an intermediate layer below the flooring, or for immediate use)
parole.testo: From Middle High German esterich, estrich, from Old High German estrih, asterih, from Late Latin astracum, astricum, from Ancient Greek ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “potsherd”).
From Latin etēsiae, from Ancient Greek ἐτήσιος (etḗsios, “annual”).

parole.significato: ethics (study of principles governing right and wrong conduct)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin ēthica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ), from ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).
Borrowed from Latin etymologia, from Ancient Greek ἐτυμολογία (etumología).
From Ecclesiastical Latin eucharistia, from Ancient Greek εὐχαριστία (eukharistía, “gratitude, giving of thanks”).

parole.significato: eucalyptus (any of many trees of genus Eucalyptus)
parole.testo: 19th century, learned borrowing from New Latin eucalyptus, coined by L’Héritier after Ancient Greek εὐ- (eu-, “well”) + καλυπτός (kaluptós, “covered”).

parole.significato: eunuch (a castrated man employed as harem guard or women’s servant)
parole.testo: In Germanised form since ca. 1600, from Late Middle High German eunuchus, from Latin eunūchus, from Ancient Greek εὐνοῦχος (eunoûkhos).
Borrowed from Latin euphonia, from Ancient Greek εὐφωνἰα (euphōnia).
From Latin evangelizō, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγελίζω (euangelízō), + -ieren.
From Latin evangelista, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγελιστής (euangelistḗs).

parole.significato: Evangelium, Gospel (one of the first four books of the New Testament: Matthew, Mark, Luke, or John)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin euangelium, evangelium, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion).
Borrowed from Latin ex-, from ē-, from Ancient Greek ἐξ- (ex-), from ἐκ- (ek-).
From Middle High German Exodus, from Latin Exodus, from Ancient Greek ἔξοδος (éxodos).
From Medieval Latin exorcizō, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκίζω (exorkízō, “to banish an evil spirit; bind by oath”), from ἐξ (ex) + ὅρκος (hórkos).
From Middle High German fantasīe (whence also the obsolete doublet Phantasei), learned borrowing from Latin phantasia, from Ancient Greek φᾰντᾰσῐ́ᾱ (phăntăsĭ́ā). Doublet of fancy and Fantasia.

parole.significato: fleam (kind of sharp instrument used for blood-letting)
parole.testo: From Middle High German vlietem(e), vliedem(e) f or m, from Old High German fliotema, fliodema f, from Latin phlebotomus, from Ancient Greek φλεβοτώμος (phlebotṓmos). In Late Middle High German, final -em becomes -en (as in Faden etc.). From this a weak-declension nominative vliete is backformed. Co
Borrowed from Medieval Latin poledrus (“a sharp-edged frame on which the suspect's feet were weighed down”), from Ancient Greek πῶλος (pôlos, “foal”).
Derived from Medieval Latin calamīna (or some Romance dialect), from Latin cadmia, ultimately from the Ancient Greek κᾰδμείᾱ, κᾰδμήᾱ, κᾰδμῐ́ᾱ (kădmeíā, kădmḗā, kădmĭ́ā, “calamine”).

parole.significato: germander (any plant of the genus Teucrium)
parole.testo: From Middle High German gamandrē, from Late Latin gamandrea, chamandrea, from Latin chamaedrys, from Ancient Greek χαμαίδρῡς (khamaídrūs, literally “ground-oak”).
Borrowed from Latin geōgraphia.
From Late Latin geōmetrēs, from Ancient Greek γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs).
Learned borrowing from Latin glottis, from Ancient Greek γλωττίς (glōttís).
From Middle High German grāmatic, grāmaticā, from Old High German grammatih, gramatih, borrowed from Latin (ars) grammatica, from Ancient Greek γραμματικὴ τέχνη (grammatikḕ tékhnē, “art of letters”).

18th century, from Grammatik + -er. Formally corresponding to Old High German grammatihhāri, gramatihhāri, which was not continued, cf. Middle High German grāmaticus. Ultimatively from Latin (ars) grammatica, from Ancient Greek γραμματικὴ τέχνη (grammatikḕ tékhnē, “art of letters”).
From Latin grammaticus, from Ancient Greek γραμματικός (grammatikós). Analysable as Grammatik + -isch.

From Middle High German grille, from Old High German grillo, probably from Latin gryllus (“grasshopper, cricket”), possibly onomatopoetic in origin, but perhaps borrowed in turn from Ancient Greek γρύλλος (grúllos, “Egyptian dance performer; painted caricature”), of unknown further origin.
From Middle High German gummi (13th c.), from Medieval Latin gummi, byform of older cummi(s), which see.

parole.significato: grammar school (UK), prep school (US) (school used to prepare students for university)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gymnasium, from Ancient Greek γυμνάσιον (gumnásion, “exercise, school”), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”).

parole.significato: halo (circular band of coloured light, visible around the Sun or Moon etc., caused by reflection and refraction of ligh…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin halo, from accusative of Latin halos, from Ancient Greek ἅλως (hálōs, “disk of the sun or moon; ring of light around the sun or moon; threshing floor with its surrounding threshold; disk of a shield”).

parole.significato: helium; the chemical element and lighest noble gas with the atomic number 2
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin hēlium, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”). The name of the gas was a derivation from the Ancient Greek term for Sun because helium was the first element to be found in the Sun's atmosphere via spectroscopy.
From Latin hēpatītis, from hēpar (“liver”), from Ancient Greek ἧπαρ (hêpar, “liver”).
18th century, from Latin hērōs, from Ancient Greek ἥρως (hḗrōs).
18th century, from Latin heterogeneus, from Ancient Greek ἑτερογενής (heterogenḗs). By surface analysis, hetero- + -gen.
From Latin hexagōnum, from Ancient Greek ἑξάγωνον (hexágōnon), substantivized neuter form of ἑξάγωνος (hexágōnos, “hexagonal”).
19th century, from Late Latin hibīscus, whence also older Eibisch.
From New Latin hīdrōsis, from Ancient Greek ῑ̔δρώς (hīdrṓs, “sweat”) + -ωσῐς (-ōsĭs).
From New Latin hīdrōsis, from Ancient Greek ῑ̔δρώς (hīdrṓs, “sweat”) + -ωσῐς (-ōsĭs).
From Latin homologia and Ancient Greek ὁμολογία (homología). By surface analysis, homo- (“homo-”) + -logie (“-logy”).

parole.significato: horizon (line where the sky appears to meet the earth; (figurative) range of someone’s thinking or insight)
parole.testo: 16th century, borrowed from Latin horizōn, horizontis, from Ancient Greek ὁρίζων (horízōn), from ὅρος (hóros, “boundary”).
From Latin horoscopium, from Ancient Greek ὡροσκοπεῖον (hōroskopeîon).
From Middle High German hundeszunge, from Old High German hunteszunga, a calque of Latin cynoglossos, itself from Ancient Greek κυνόγλωσσον (kunóglōsson). By surface analysis, Hund + -s- + Zunge.
Borrowed from Latin hymnus, from Ancient Greek ὕμνος (húmnos).
From Late Latin hypnoticus, from Ancient Greek ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós, “inclined to sleep, putting to sleep, sleepy”), from ὑπνῶ (hupnô, “I put to sleep”), from ὕπνος (húpnos, “sleep”).
Borrowed from Latin hypothēca (“pledge, mortgage”), from Ancient Greek ὑποθήκη (hupothḗkē, “warning, pledge”).

Borrowed from Latin hyaena, from Ancient Greek ὕαινα (húaina). At first also hientier (15th century). According to Pliny, precious stones called hyaenia are won from hyena eyes, whence Middle High German hiennia (“kind of gem”), perhaps already Old High German hiena (“handle made of gemstone”).
From Latin haemorrhoidae, from Ancient Greek αἱμορροίδες (haimorrhoídes), from αἱμόρροος (haimórrhoos, “flowing with blood”), from αἷμα (haîma, “blood”) and the root of ῥέω (rhéō, “flow”).
From Medieval Latin haeresis, from Ancient Greek αἵρεσις (haíresis, “taking, receiving; choice”).
From Medieval Latin haereticus (from Ancient Greek αἱρετῐκός (hairetĭkós)) + -isch.
Borrowed from Latin īdōlum, from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon). Used in German chiefly since the 18th century, before that occasionally as an ad-hoc borrowing from the Latin.
Borrowed from Latin icterus, from Ancient Greek ἴκτερος (íkteros, “jaundice”).
Borrowed from Latin isthmus.
Borrowed from Latin ïambus, from Ancient Greek ἴαμβος (íambos).

parole.significato: The letter J in the Latin and German alphabet.
parole.testo: From Latin iota, from Ancient Greek ἰῶτα (iôta), from Semitic yodh (the tenth letter of many Semitic alphabets), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *yad- (“hand”)
From Latin Judas, from Ancient Greek Ἰούδας (Ioúdas), from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (yəhūḏā).

Inherited from Middle High German jude, jüde, from Old High German judo, judeo, from Latin iūdaeus (“Judaean, Jew”), from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), derived from Ἰουδά (Ioudá, “Judah”) + -ιος (-ios), the former from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (yəhūḏāh).

From Middle High German jüdisch (judisch, jüdesch, judesch), from Old High German judeisc, derived from judo, judeo + -isc, the former from Latin iūdaeus (“Judaean, Jew”), from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), derived from Ἰουδά (Ioudá, “Judah”) + -ιος (-ios), the former from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (yəhū
Borrowed from Latin cachecticus.

parole.significato: tile (on walls or floors or stovetops, not roof tile)
parole.testo: From Middle High German kachel, kachele, from Old High German chachala, from Vulgar Latin *cacculus, from cāccabus (“cooking pot”), from Ancient Greek κάκκαβος (kákkabos, “a pot or a pan”). Cognate with Alemannic German Kakel.
Borrowed from Latin cactus, from Ancient Greek κάκτος (káktos, “cardoon”), of pre-Greek origin.

parole.significato: sweet flag, Acorus calamus, an herbal water plant
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle High German kalmus, from Latin calamus.

parole.significato: canon (selection of texts considered accepted and/or authentic)
parole.testo: From Latin canōn, from Ancient Greek κανών (kanṓn, “measuring rod, standard”).

parole.significato: canon (member of certain bodies in subject to an ecclesiastical rule)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin canonicus + -er, from Ancient Greek κανονικός (kanonikós).

parole.significato: catalogue (systematic list of names, books, pictures, etc.; complete list of items; university calendar)
parole.testo: From Late Latin catalogus, from Ancient Greek κατάλογος (katálogos, “an enrollment, a register”), from καταλέγω (katalégō, “to recount, to tell at length”), from κατά (katá, “downwards, towards”) + λέγω (légō, “to gather, to pick up, to choose for oneself, to pick out, to count”).
From Latin catapulta.
Borrowed from Latin catarrhus, from Ancient Greek κατάρροος (katárrhoos).
From Latin catastropha (“turning-point of an action, catastrophe”), from Ancient Greek καταστροφή (katastrophḗ, “overturning”).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin catēchēsis, from Ancient Greek κατήχησις (katḗkhēsis), from κατηχέω (katēkhéō), from κατά (katá) + ἠχή (ēkhḗ).
From Late Latin catēgoria (compare Yiddish קאַטעגאָריע (kategorye)), from Ancient Greek κατηγορία (katēgoría).
16th century, from Latin cathedra, from Ancient Greek καθέδρα (kathédra).
From Cathetus (18th century), from Latin cathetus (15th century). Ultimately from Ancient Greek κάθετος (káthetos, “perpendicular”).

parole.significato: catheter (small tube inserted into a body cavity)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin catheter, from Ancient Greek καθετήρ (kathetḗr).
Borrowed from Latin catholicus.
From Middle High German kervel, from Old High German kervil, from Latin caerefolium, chaerephyllum, from Ancient Greek χαιρέφυλλον (khairéphullon).

parole.significato: clergy (mainly used for the Christian clergy, sometimes for the clergy of other religions)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin clērus, from Ancient Greek κλῆρος (klêros).
Borrowed from Late Latin clysterium, from Latin clyster, from Ancient Greek κλυστήρ (klustḗr).
Borrowed from Latin colon.
From Early New High German Colofonie, from Latin (resina) Colophōnia, from Ancient Greek Κολοφών (Kolophṓn), an ancient city in Ionia.
16th century semi-learned borrowing from Latin colossus, from Ancient Greek κολοσσός (kolossós).
Borrowed from Latin comma.
Borrowed from Latin cōmoedia.
Borrowed from Latin crisis.

parole.significato: crystal in the sense of mineral and its molecular structure ("array of atoms"), not in the sense of glass / glassware (…
parole.testo: From Middle High German kristal, kristalle, from Old High German cristalla, from Latin crystallum, from Ancient Greek κρύσταλλος (krústallos, “ice”). Cognate with Vilamovian kryśtaoł.
Borrowed from Latin critērium, critērion, from Ancient Greek κριτήριον (kritḗrion).
Learned borrowing from Latin crocus, from Ancient Greek κρόκος (krókos).
Borrowed from Latin crypta, from Ancient Greek κρυπτή (kruptḗ), female form of the adjective κρυπτός (kruptós).
From Late Latin crypticus, with assimilation to native suffix -isch, from Ancient Greek κρυπτικός (kruptikós). Cognate to English cryptic.
Borrowed from Latin Croesus, from Ancient Greek Κροῖσος (Kroîsos).
Learned borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin Kȳrie eleison, borrowed from Ancient Greek Κῡ́ριε ἐλέησον (Kū́rie eléēson, “Lord, have mercy”).

From Middle High German chafter (“beehive; little chamber, closet”), from Old High German chafteri (“beehive”), from Medieval Latin capistērium (“beehive”), for scaphistērium, from Ancient Greek σκαφιστήριον (skaphistḗrion).
From Middle High German latwārje, latwērje, from Late Latin ēlectuārium, from Ancient Greek ἐκλείκτον (ekleíkton, “medicine which is licked away”). Compare Hungarian and Slovak lekvár (“jam”).
From New Latin, from Latin laudō (“to praise”), or ladanum (“a gum resin”), from Ancient Greek λάδανον (ládanon).
From Middle High German līre, from Old High German līra, from Latin lyra, from Ancient Greek λύρα (lúra).
From the Latin lemma, from the Ancient Greek λῆμμᾰ (lêmmă).
From Middle High German litanīe, from Late Latin litanīa, from Ancient Greek λιτανεία (litaneía).

parole.significato: lithium; the chemical element and lightest alkali metal with the atomic number 3
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin lithium, from Ancient Greek λίθος (líthos, “stone”) as this element was the first alkali metal to be found in stones instead of plants.
Borrowed from Latin logica, from Ancient Greek λογική (logikḗ, “logic”).
Borrowed from Latin lotos, from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós).

From Latin Lycēum, from Ancient Greek Λύκειον (Lúkeion). The use for a girls’ school may have been partly due to an inhibition to using the word Gymnasium with girls because of the underlying Ancient Greek γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”).
From New Latin magnēsium, from Ancient Greek μαγνησία (magnēsía), after Μαγνησία (Magnēsía, “Magnesia”).
From Middle High German mange, mangel, from Latin manganum, from Ancient Greek μάγγᾰνον (mángănon).
16th century, from Latin mania, from Ancient Greek μανία (manía).
Borrowed from Latin marmor, from Ancient Greek μάρμαρος (mármaros, “marble, crystalline rock”). Doublet of Murmel.
From Middle High German masse, from Late Old High German massa, from Latin massa.
From Latin mēchanicus.
Learned borrowing from New Latin mechanismus, from Ancient Greek μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “machine”).

Learned borrowing from Latin Megaera, from Ancient Greek Μέγαιρα (Mégaira), from μεγαίρω (megaírō, “to grudge, to envy”). For the usage as a common noun, cf. German mégère, Italian megera and Russian меге́ра (megéra).

From Latin melancholicus, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολικός (melankholikós, “atrabilious, impulsive, of atrabilious or melancholic temperament”), from μελαγχολία (melankholía, “melancholy”). By surface analysis, Melancholie + -isch.

parole.significato: melody, tune (sequence of notes that makes up a musical phrase)
parole.testo: From Middle High German melodīe, from Latin melodia, from Ancient Greek μελῳδίᾱ (melōidíā). Since the 16th century, the inherited form Melodei was increasingly readapted to the Latin and to French mélodie.

parole.significato: The Messiah / messiah (Jesus Christ, Jesus the Messiah, Jesus the Christ).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Messīās, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek Μεσσίας (Messías), from Aramaic משיחא (məšīḥā), from Biblical Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ (māšîaḥ, “anointed”).

parole.significato: meteor (streak of light caused by extraterrestrial matter entering the atmosphere)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin meteōrum, from Ancient Greek μετέωρον (metéōron), neuter of μετέωρος (metéōros, “up in the air”).
Borrowed from Latin methodus f, from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos).
From Latin methodicus, from Ancient Greek μεθοδικός (methodikós). Morphologically analyzable as Methode (“method”) + -isch.
From Late Latin metonymia, from Ancient Greek μετωνυμίᾱ (metōnumíā, “change of name”), from μετά (metá, “other”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).
Borrowed from Latin mētropolis, from Ancient Greek μητρόπολις (mētrópolis).
Borrowed from Latin metrum, derived from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron). Doublet of Meter.
From Latin mīmicus, from Ancient Greek μῑμικός (mīmikós, “belonging to mimes”), from μῖμος (mîmos, “imitator, actor”); attested since 18th century.

From Middle High German mitelīden, first used in mystic literature as a calque of Latin compassiō (“compassion”), itself a calque of Ancient Greek συμπάθεια (sumpátheia, “compassion, sympathy”). By surface analysis, mit (“with”) + Leid (“sorrow, suffering”). From Middle High German is borrowed Dutch

parole.significato: mitre (headgear worn on solemn occasions by church dignitaries)
parole.testo: From Latin mitra, from Ancient Greek μίτρα (mítra, “headband, turban”).
Borrowed from Latin monarchia, from Ancient Greek μοναρχία (monarkhía).
From Medieval Latin moschus, alternative form of muscus, from Ancient Greek μόσχος (móskhos), from Middle Persian [script needed] (mwšk' /⁠mušk⁠⁠/).
Learned borrowing from Latin mūraena, mūrēna, from Ancient Greek μύραινα (múraina). Attested since the 14th century, sometimes also borrowed as Mure (18th century). Not related to German Maräne.

parole.significato: museum (building or institution dedicated to the protection and exhibition of items with scientific, historical, cultur…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mūsēum (“library, study”), from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον (Mouseîon), shrine of the Muses (Μοῦσα (Moûsa)).

parole.significato: myrobalan, any of the three myrobalans and further the whole genus Terminalia and any tree of any species in it
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin myrobalanus f, from Ancient Greek μυροβάλανος (murobálanos).

16th-century relatinization of older Mirre, from Middle High German mirre, from Old High German mirra, myrra, from Ecclesiastical Latin myrrha, from Ancient Greek μύρρᾱ (múrrhā), from a Semitic language.
16th-century relatinization of older Mirtel, Mirten, from Middle High German mirtel, from Old High German mirtil, from Latin myrtus, from Ancient Greek μύρτος (múrtos, “myrtle”).
Borrowed from Latin mysticus.

parole.significato: meander (one of a series of regular sinuous curves, bends, loops, turns, or windings in the channel of a river, stream,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Maeander, from Ancient Greek Μαίανδρος (Maíandros) – a river in Asia Minor (present day Turkey) known for its winding course.

From Middle High German münster, from Old High German munistiuri (8th century), from Vulgar Latin *monisterium, from Latin monastērium, from Ancient Greek μοναστήριον (monastḗrion). Cognate with English minster and the doublet monastery, and Sicilian misteri.

parole.significato: to copy, imitate, emulate (a person or thing)
parole.testo: nach- + ahmen, the latter from Middle High German āmen (“to gauge”), from Middle High German āme, ōme (“liquid measure”), borrowed from Latin ama, hama (“firebucket, pail”), ultimately from Ancient Greek ἄμη (ámē, “water-bucket”).
From Middle High German narde, from Old High German narda (9th c.), from Latin nardus, from Ancient Greek νάρδος (nárdos), from a Semitic language.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin narcōticum (“narcotic”, neuter singular), from Ancient Greek ναρκωτικός (narkōtikós), from ναρκόω (narkóō, “to numb”).

parole.significato: neophyte, invasive species (recently introduced plant species)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin neophytus, from Ancient Greek νεόφυτος (neóphutos, “newly planted”).

parole.significato: nickel (a silvery elemental metal with an atomic number of 28 and symbol Ni).
parole.testo: A pet form of the proper masculine name Nikolaus, see also Old Nick "the devil", Nickel, and Nicholas. See Kupfernickel for more.

parole.significato: a representation of St. Nicholas (e.g. an actor or a figurine)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Nīcolāus. Compare English Nicholas.
From Nil (“Nile”) + Pferd (“horse”), a loose calque of Latin hippopotamus, from Ancient Greek ἱπποπόταμος (hippopótamos). Akin to Dutch nijlpaard.
Borrowed from New Latin nostalgia, from Ancient Greek νόστος (nóstos, “a return home”) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain, suffering”), translating German Heimweh.
Borrowed from Latin obolus, from Ancient Greek ὀβολός (obolós).
From Middle High German ocker, ogger, from Old High German ockar, from Latin ōchra, from Ancient Greek ὤχρα (ṓkhra, “pale yellow”), from ὠχρός (ōkhrós, “pale, ocher”) (modern Greek ωχρός (ochrós)).

parole.significato: ode, poem of a certain type
parole.testo: From Latin ode
From Latin Odyssēa, from Ancient Greek Ὀδύσσεια (Odússeia).
From Latin oleum (“olive oil”), from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion, “olive oil”). Doublet of Öl.
Borrowed from Latin oneirologia, from Ancient Greek ὄνειρος (óneiros) + -λογία (-logía).
Borrowed from Latin onyx.

parole.significato: Ide, a fish of species Leuciscus idus (syn. Leuciscus orfus)
parole.testo: From Latin orphus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφώς (orphṓs, “dusky grouper”).
Borrowed from Latin orgasmus, from Ancient Greek ὀργασμός (orgasmós).
Borrowed from Late Latin orthodoxus, from Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos), from ὀρθός (orthós, “straight”) + δόξα (dóxa, “opinion”).
Borrowed from Latin orthographia, from Ancient Greek ὀρθογρᾰφῐ́ᾱ (orthogrăphĭ́ā).
Learned borrowing from Latin ōceanus, from Ancient Greek ὠκεανός (ōkeanós).

parole.significato: panther, black panther (a leopard or other big cat with black fur)
parole.testo: From Middle High German panter, pantel, from Latin panthera, from Ancient Greek πάνθηρ (pánthēr).
From Middle High German paradīs(e), from Old High German paradīs, from Latin paradīsum. The modern form with -ie- perhaps partly from non-diphthongising dialects, but chiefly after the Latin.
16th century, from Latin paradigma, from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma).
Borrowed from Latin parallēlus, parallēlos, from Ancient Greek παράλληλος (parállēlos).
From Latin paralysis, from Ancient Greek παράλυσις (parálusis).
Borrowed from Latin pardalis, from Ancient Greek πάρδαλις (párdalis). Compare English pard.
From Latin parenthesis, from Ancient Greek παρένθεσις (parénthesis).
From New Latin paresis, from Ancient Greek πάρεσις (páresis, “letting go, paralysis”).
From French parodie + -ieren, from Latin parōdia, from Ancient Greek παρῳδία (parōidía).

parole.significato: paroxysm (random or sudden outburst; explosive event during a volcanic eruption; sudden recurrence of a disease)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin paroxysmus, from Ancient Greek παροξυσμός (paroxusmós, “irritation, the severe fit of a disease”).
From Latin pascha.

parole.significato: paten (plate used to hold the host during the Eucharist)
parole.testo: Middle High German patēne, Old High German phatena, Ecclesiastical Latin patena, Ancient Greek πατάνη (patánē, “kind of flat dish”). Doublet of Patina.
From Middle High German pellicān, from Latin pelicānus, pelecānus, from Ancient Greek πελεκάν (pelekán).
Borrowed from Late Latin perinaeum, from Ancient Greek περίναιον (perínaion).
Borrowed from Latin Petrus.

From Middle High German phingesten, from Late Latin pentēcostē, from Ancient Greek πεντηκοστή (pentēkostḗ). The Old High German form fimfchusti is a partial calque of the Ancient Greek term, with πεντη- (pentē-) replaced by fimf (“five”). Cognate with Hunsrik Pingste and Dutch Pinksteren.
Borrowed from New Latin pharynx, from Ancient Greek φᾰ́ρῠγξ (phắrŭnx, “throat”).
From Middle High German philosophīe, from Latin philosophia, which see. Not fully integrated during the Middle High German period; therefore the inherited form in -ei did not establish itself.
Borrowed from Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”).
Borrowed from Latin pinacothēca, from Ancient Greek πινακοθήκη (pinakothḗkē).
Borrowed from Late Latin pistācia.

From Middle High German plānēte, a loanword from Latin planeta, planetes, from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs), a variant of πλάνης (plánēs, “wanderer”). The German term Wandelstern is a calque of the former.
From Late Latin plasma (literally “mold”), from Ancient Greek πλάσμα (plásma, “something formed”).
Borrowed from Late Latin pleonasmus, from Ancient Greek πλεονασμός (pleonasmós, “abundance; excess”).
From French plombe + -ieren, from plomb, from Latin plumbum, from Ancient Greek μόλυβδος (mólubdos, “lead”).
From Old High German pletta, probably from Vulgar Latin *platta, *plattus, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “wide; flat”); if so doublet of Platte. Not attested in Middle High German.
From Latin podium, from Ancient Greek πόδιον (pódion, “foot of vase”), diminutive of πούς (poús, “foot”).
From Middle High German poēte, from Latin poēta, from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs, “creator, composer”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin policia, from Late Latin polītīa.
From Latin polyhistor (“very learned”), from Hellenistic Ancient Greek πολυΐστωρ (poluḯstōr, “greatly learned”).
Borrowed from Latin polypus.

Borrowed from Latin porus. Pfeifer explains the change in gender as a backformation of the plural Poren in the second half of 18th century. Kluge says it was borrowed in the 15th century, presumably referring to earlier plural use.

parole.significato: internship (job taken by a student), apprenticeship
parole.testo: From the neuter of Late Latin practicus (“practical”), from Ancient Greek πρακτικός (praktikós, “of or pertaining to action, concerned with action or business, active, practical”), from πράσσω (prássō, “I do”).
18th century, from Latin prognosis, from Ancient Greek πρόγνωσις (prógnōsis).

parole.significato: procope, apheresis (loss of an initial vowel)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin procope, from Ancient Greek προκοπή (prokopḗ).
Borrowed from Latin prophēta, from Ancient Greek προφήτης (prophḗtēs).

From Middle High German prophētīe, from Latin prophētīa, from Ancient Greek προφητεία (prophēteía). By surface analysis, Prophet + -ie. The regular forms are those in -ei, the contemporary vocalism is due to learned relatinization.
From Latin prosōdia.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin prōstata, from Ancient Greek προστάτης (prostátēs, “one standing before, protector”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).

parole.significato: a copy of the Psalms independent from the rest of the Old Testament (either on its own or along with the New Testament)
parole.testo: From Middle High German salter, from Old High German saltāri, from Latin psaltērium, from Ancient Greek ψαλτήριον (psaltḗrion). The modern Ps- is due to relatinization; see Psalm for more.
Borrowed from Latin psȳchopompus.

parole.significato: Pygmy, pygmy (member of one of various Ancient Equatorial African tribal peoples, notable for their very short stature)
parole.testo: From Latin Pygmaeī, from Ancient Greek πυγμαῖος (pugmaîos, “a member of a race of dwarves”), from πυγμή (pugmḗ, “fist (as small as a fist)”).

15th century, as Pyramis, from Latin pyramis, from Ancient Greek πυραμίς (puramís). The modern form since ca. 1600 from the Graeco-Latin inflected stem (genitive pyramidis, πυραμίδος), possibly after Middle French pyramide.
From Latin pyrōpus, from Ancient Greek πυρωπός (purōpós, “fiery-eyed, fire-colored”), from πῦρ (pûr, “fire”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”); compare French pyrope.
Borrowed from Latin paedagogus, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós), from παῖς (paîs, “child”) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “guide”).

From Middle High German quiten, from Old High German quitina, from Vulgar Latin *quidonia, from Classical Latin cotōneum, cydōnium or malum cydonium, from Ancient Greek κῠδώνῐον (kŭdṓnĭon) an elipsis from κυδώνια μῆλα, μηλοκῠδώνῐον (kudṓnia mêla, mēlokŭdṓnĭon). Cognate with Dutch kwee.

Late 16th or early 17th century calque of Latin ortographia, from Ancient Greek ὀρθογρᾰφῐ́ᾱ (orthogrăphĭ́ā); compare Old High German rehtscrībāri (“person who writes correctly”), itself a calque of Latin orthographus. By surface analysis, recht (“proper, correct”) + Schreibung (“spelling”)
From Middle High German rīs, borrowed from Late Latin rīsum or rīsus, from Latin orȳza, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὄρῡζα (órūza) (Greek όρυζα (óryza)). See also English rice.
From Middle High German rhetorica/retorica, from Latin rhētorica, from Ancient Greek ῥητορικός (rhētorikós). Compare French rhétorique.
Early 18th century, from Latin rheuma, from Ancient Greek ῥεῦμα (rheûma).
Early 18th century, from Latin rheumatismus, from Ancient Greek ῥευματισμός (rheumatismós).

From Middle High German rinōceros, from Latin rhīnocerōs, from Ancient Greek ῥῑνόκερως (rhīnókerōs, literally “nose-horned”). The inflected forms in -rosses, -rösser are by association with unrelated Ross (“horse”); the same might also apply to the neuter gender.

parole.significato: rhomboid (A parallelogram which is neither a rhombus nor a rectangle)
parole.testo: From Latin rhomboīdēs, from Ancient Greek ῥομβοειδής (rhomboeidḗs, “rhombus-shaped”, “rhomboidal”). Equivalent to Rhombus + -oid.
From Middle High German sabbat, sābāot, sābot, from Latin sabbatum, from Ancient Greek σάββατον (sábbaton), from Hebrew שַׁבָּת (shabát, “Sabbath”).
From Middle High German zisma, from Latin schisma, from Ancient Greek σχίσμα (skhísma, “division”), from σχίζω (skhízō, “to split”).

parole.significato: A dark brown pigment made from the secretions of the cuttlefish; sepia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sēpia.
Latin Sibylla, from Ancient Greek Σίβυλλα (Síbulla).

parole.significato: scope (region of an utterance to which some modifying element applies)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin scopus.

From Middle High German scorpiōn, schorpiōn, relatinised variants of older schorpe, from Old High German scorpio, from Latin scorpio, from Ancient Greek σκορπίων (skorpíōn), variant of σκορπίος (skorpíos).

From Middle High German smaract, from Latin smaragdus, from Ancient Greek σμάραγδος (smáragdos), μάραγδος (máragdos), from a Semitic language. Also written schmaragd in Early Modern German, and still widely so pronounced until the diffusion of the Siebs standard.
Borrowed from Latin smēgma.

parole.significato: a form of sexual intercourse considered perverse and unnatural; sodomy
parole.testo: From Late Latin sodomia, from the Biblical town Sodom (Genesis 18f.), from Ancient Greek Σόδομα (Sódoma), from Hebrew סדם (səḏōm).
Borrowed from Latin soloecismus.

From 15th-century Middle High German sparge, spargen, sparges, from Medieval Latin sparagus, asparagus, in part through Italian sparago, sparagio. The form in -el (16th c.) probably after such plant names as Kerbel, Kümmel.
Of uncertain origin. Perhaps from late Medieval Latin sparta, from Ancient Greek σπάρτη (spártē, “hereditament”).
Borrowed from Latin spēlunca, from Ancient Greek σπῆλυγξ (spêlunx, “cave, cavern, grotto”). Cognate to English spelunk
Borrowed from Latin sperma, from Ancient Greek σπέρμα (spérma, “seed, semen”).
Borrowed from Late Latin sphēra.
From Latin spondēus, from Ancient Greek σπονδεῖος (spondeîos).
New Latin spora, from Ancient Greek σπορά (sporá).
16th century, from Stachel (“spine, spike”) + Schwein (“pig, swine”), a calque of Latin porcus spīnōsus, itself a calque of Ancient Greek ἀκανθόχοιρος (akanthókhoiros).
Borrowed from Latin stadium.

parole.significato: a loose scarf, wrap, worn on top of other clothes
parole.testo: Relatinization of older Stole, from Middle High German stōl(e), from Old High German stōla (since ca. 800), borrowed from Latin stola, from Ancient Greek στολή (stolḗ).
From Latin stratēgus, from Ancient Greek στρατηγός (stratēgós), possibly influenced by French stratège.
From Latin stratum (“covering, blanket”) + Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, sphere”).
Inherited from Middle High German strūȥ, strūȥe, from Old High German strūȥ, borrowed from Latin strūthiō, from Ancient Greek στρουθίων (strouthíōn).
Borrowed from Latin stropha, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek στροφή (strophḗ, “a turn, bend, twist”).
Learned borrowing from Latin syllēpsis, from Ancient Greek σύλληψις (súllēpsis).
Borrowed from Latin syllogismus, from Ancient Greek συλλογισμός (sullogismós, “inference, conclusion”).

First attested in 1657. Borrowed from New Latin sylphes, coined by Paracelsus in the 16th century. The coinage may derive from Latin sylvestris (“of the woods”) and nympha (“nymph”), or otherwise Ancient Greek σίλφη (sílphē, “beetle”). More at sylph.
Borrowed from Latin symmetria, from Ancient Greek συμμετρία (summetría).
Borrowed from Latin sympathia, from Ancient Greek συμπάθεια (sumpátheia).
Borrowed from Latin symphōnia. Doublet of Sinfonie.

From Middle High German sinagoge, from Latin synagoga, from Ancient Greek συναγωγή (sunagōgḗ). Used in German texts since the 12th century, but mainly a learned word. The popular term was Judenschule; compare Yiddish שול (shul).
Borrowed from Late Latin synchronus in the first half of the 19th century, from Ancient Greek σύγχρονος (súnkhronos, “contemporary; synchronous; simultaneous”).

parole.significato: synchysis (Confused arrangement of words in a sentence.)
parole.testo: From older Synchysis, learned borrowing from Latin synchysis, from Ancient Greek σύγχυσις (súnkhusis, “a mixing”).

parole.significato: a lawyer permanently employed by a company (or other organization), an in-house counsel
parole.testo: 15th century, from Latin syndicus, from Ancient Greek σύνδικος (súndikos). At first in northern usage and thus chiefly through Middle Low German sindicus (13th c.). Compare English syndic.
Learned borrowing from New Latin syndrome, from Ancient Greek συνδρομή (sundromḗ).
Borrowed from Latin synecdoche, from Ancient Greek συνεκδοχή (sunekdokhḗ, “receiving together”).
Learned borrowing from Latin syncope, from Ancient Greek σῠγκοπή (sŭnkopḗ).
Borrowed from New Latin syncretismus, from late Ancient Greek συγκρητισμός (sunkrētismós).
Borrowed from Late Latin synodālis, from synodus, from Ancient Greek σύνοδος (súnodos, “assembly, meeting”). Cognate with English synodal, Dutch synodaal, French synodal.
From Latin synōnymum, from Ancient Greek συνώνυμον (sunṓnumon).
Borrowed from Latin systēma, from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma).
Borrowed from New Latin systola, from Ancient Greek συστολή (sustolḗ), from συστέλλειν (sustéllein, “to contract”), from σύν (sún, “together”) + στέλλειν (stéllein, “send”).
From Latin sc(a)ena, from Ancient Greek σκηνή (skēnḗ).

parole.significato: wallpaper (paper-like covering applied to interior walls)
parole.testo: 15th century. From Latin tapēte (“wall hanging cloth”), from tapēs (“carpet”), from Ancient Greek τάπης (tápēs, “carpet, rug”).
Borrowed from Late Latin tautologia, from Ancient Greek ταὐτολογία (tautología); compare English tautology.
From Latin tectonicus, from Ancient Greek τεκτονικός (tektonikós). By surface analysis, Tektonik + -isch.
Borrowed from Latin tetrarchēs, from Ancient Greek τετράρχης (tetrárkhēs), from τετρα- (tetra-, “four”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “ruler, leader”).
From Middle High German thema (14th c.), from Latin thema, from Ancient Greek θέμα (théma).
Borrowed from Latin theologia, from Ancient Greek θεολογία (theología). By surface analysis, theo- + -logie.
Borrowed from Late Latin theōrēma, from Ancient Greek θεώρημα (theṓrēma, “speculation, proposition to be proved”) (Euclid).
From taxonomic New Latin Thuja, from Ancient Greek θυία (thuía).

From Middle High German thimiān, alteration of thymiāme, from Latin thymiama, from Ancient Greek θυμίαμα (thumíama, “incense”). The sense through association with thymum, θύμον (thúmon, “thyme”), probably already in Latin (if not Greek itself), as thyme was a commonly used incense. Whether the two w
Borrowed from Latin Tītān, Tītānus, from Ancient Greek Τιτάν (Titán).
From Middle High German tōn, from Latin tonus, from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos).

From Middle High German topāʒje, topāʒe, topaʒīus m or n, from Late Latin topāzius f, topāzion n, topāzōn m, from Classical topāzus f, topāzos f, from Ancient Greek τοπάζιον n (topázion), τόπαζος m (tópazos), probably named after Τόπαζος (Tópazos), ancient name of St. John's Island, Egypt, in the Re

From Latin tragoedia, from Ancient Greek τραγῳδία (tragōidía, “epic play, tragedy”), from τράγος (trágos, “male goat”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”), a reference to the goat-satyrs of the theatrical plays of the Dorians.
Borrowed from Latin trapezium, from Ancient Greek τρᾰπέζῐον (trăpézĭon, “irregular quadrilateral”, literally “small table”), diminutive of τρᾰ́πεζα (trắpeza, “table”).
Ultimately from Latin tri- and Ancient Greek τρι- (tri-, “three”).

parole.significato: triglyph (vertically channeled tablet of the Doric frieze)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin triglyphus, from Ancient Greek τρίγλυφος (trígluphos).
From 1610s, from New Latin trigōnometria, from Ancient Greek τρίγωνον (trígōnon, “triangle”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”).
From Latin trochaeus, from Ancient Greek τροχαῖος (trokhaîos).
Borrowed from Latin tornus.
Borrowed from Latin typus (“figure, pattern”), from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “type; impression”). Compare French type (“guy, bloke”), and Spanish tipo.
19th century, from Latin typhus, from Ancient Greek τῦφος (tûphos).

From un- (“un-”) + Mittel (“means, medium”) + -bar (“-able, -ly”), 17th-century alteration of Middle High German unmittelich, calque of Latin immediatus, itself a calque of Ancient Greek ἄμεσος (ámesos).
Named after the planet Uranus, from Latin Ūranus.
From Latin ūrīna, from Ancient Greek οὖρον (oûron).

parole.significato: Lord's Prayer; Our Father; paternoster (prayer that Jesus taught his disciples)
parole.testo: Univerbation of the prayer’s first two words Vater unser: From Middle High German vatir unsir etc., from Old High German fater unser, translation of Latin Pater noster, itself translated from Ancient Greek πάτερ ἡμῶν (páter hēmôn). The postposition of the possessive was still grammatical in Old High
Vorsteher (“one that stands before”) + Drüse (“gland”), the first element being a semantic loan from Latin prostata, itself from Ancient Greek προστάτης (prostátēs).
Weisheit + -s- + Zahn, literally “wisdom tooth”. Calque of Latin dēns sapientae, itself calqued from Ancient Greek σωφρονιστῆρες (sōphronistêres). See English wisdom tooth for cognates.
From Middle High German isôpe, ysôpe, from Old High German isopo, isipo, variant declension of hysop, from Medieval Latin hȳsōpus, hȳssōpus, from Latin hȳsōpum, from Ancient Greek ὕσσωπος (hússōpos).
From Middle High German zēder, cēder, from Old High German cēdar, from Latin cedrus, from Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros).

parole.significato: zealot (member of the Zealot movement in Judea)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin zēlōtēs, from Ancient Greek ζηλωτής (zēlōtḗs). See zealot.
From Late Middle High German zentrum (also zenter), from Latin centrum (“centre”), from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron, “centre of a circle, thorn”).
Borrowed from Latin Zephyrus, from Ancient Greek Ζέφυρος (Zéphuros, “Zephyrus, the west wind”).
Borrowed from Latin Cerberus, from Ancient Greek Κέρβερος (Kérberos).
Borrowed from Latin zeta and Ancient Greek ζῆτα (zêta). Doublet of Zett.
Borrowed from Latin cibōrium, from Ancient Greek κιβώριον (kibṓrion).
From Latin cymbalum, from Ancient Greek κύμβαλον (kúmbalon). Doublet of Zimbal.

From late Middle High German zimet, from earlier zinemīn, zinment, from Latin cinnamon, cinnamomum, from Ancient Greek κιννάμωμον (kinnámōmon), later κίνναμον (kínnamon), according to Herodotus from Phoenician, cognate with Hebrew קִנָּמוֹן (qinnāmōn).
Borrowed from Latin circus.
See late Middle High German zitterlein. From Old High German zithara, from Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára). See also Gitarre.

From Middle High German Tzwetzschken, ultimately from the Vulgar Latin plural form *davascena, from Latin damascēna n pl (“damascene plums”), from Ancient Greek δαμασκηνά (damaskēná, “ibid.”) itself from Ancient Greek Δαμασκός (Damaskós, “Damascus”).

parole.significato: cyclic (characterized by, or moving in cycles)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cyclicus, from Ancient Greek κυκλικός (kuklikós) + -isch.
Borrowed from Latin cylindrus, from Ancient Greek κῠ́λινδρος (kŭ́lindros).
From Middle High German zipresse, zipressenboum, from Old High German cipresenboum, from Latin cypressus, cupressus, from Ancient Greek κυπάρισσος (kupárissos).
From neo-Latin cytus (“cell”), from Ancient Greek κύτος (kútos, “a hollow”).
From Middle High German zolnære, from Old High German zolōnāri, borrowed from Medieval Latin telonarius, from telōnium (“tollbooth”).
Borrowed from Latin aegis (“shield”), from Ancient Greek αἰγῐ́ς (aigĭ́s). Doublet of Ägis.

parole.significato: aeon, eon (exceedingly long period of time)
parole.testo: 18th century, from Latin aeōn (“age, eternity”), from Ancient Greek αἰών (aiṓn, “age, eternity”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyu- (“vital force, life, long life, eternity”).

parole.significato: aesthetics (the study of art or beauty)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αἰσθητικός (aisthētikós).
16th century, from Latin aethēr, from Ancient Greek αἰθήρ (aithḗr).
From Latin aetiologia, from Ancient Greek αἰτιολογίᾱ (aitiologíā).
From New Latin edema, from Ancient Greek οἴδημα (oídēma, “swelling”).
From Late Latin oeconomus, from Ancient Greek οἰκονόμος (oikonómos)
From Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía, “management of a household, administration”), from οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) + νόμος (nómos, “law”) (by surface analysis, öko- + -nomie).
